questions.cardText:
[Zoology] Why do some animals have a “third eyelid”?
A. To protect the eyes
B. To improve motion detection
C. To help focus on distant objects
Answer: A. The third eyelid, or nictitating membrane, can protect birds’ eyes from dust when they fly and shield sharks’ eyes from injury when they hunt prey, all while allowing clear vision.
questions.de: Wie heißt das durchsichtige „dritte Augenlid“, das die Augen von Vögeln, Haien und manchen Säugetieren schützt?
questions.en: What is the name of the transparent “third eyelid” that protects the eyes of birds, sharks and some mammals?

timeline.labelEn: Darwin's The Descent of Man cites the human semilunar fold as a vestige of the nictitating membrane
timeline.labelDe: Darwins „Die Abstammung des Menschen“ nennt die halbmondförmige Falte im Auge als Überrest der Nickhaut

questions.notes: Card's question is a 'why' with options; asked for the name of the protective structure the explanation gives.

questions.cardText:
[Literature] What kind of figure of speech is “He runs like the wind”?
A. Analogy
B. Simile
C. Metaphor
Answer: B. A simile compares two different things using the words “like” or “as.” An analogy explains a relationship between two things, such as comparing the structure of an atom to the solar system. A metaphor directly states that one thing is another, like “Time is a thief.”
questions.de: Welches Stilmittel, etwa „Er läuft wie der Wind“, vergleicht zwei verschiedene Dinge mit den Wörtern „wie“ oder „als“?
questions.en: What figure of speech, such as “He runs like the wind”, compares two different things using the words “like” or “as”?

timeline.labelEn: The word “simile” (from Latin similis, “like”) is first attested in English
timeline.labelDe: Das Wort „simile“ (von lateinisch similis, „ähnlich“) ist erstmals im Englischen belegt

questions.notes: German term: Vergleich (rhetorisch), also 'Simile'. First attestation date from Wiktionary.
